# The Model {#sec-model}

## Specification

We observe $N=4{,}586$ player-season records: $I=1{,}529$ outfield players, $S=12$ La Liga
seasons (2011–2023), $P=48$ Z-scaled performance features (goalkeepers excluded; 23 features
transformed with log1p or sqrt before scaling to reduce right skew).

The additive decomposition is:
$$
y_n = a_{i[n]} + b_{j[n]} + \varepsilon_n
$$

- $a_i\in\mathbb{R}^P$: **player effect** — stable latent identity
- $b_j\in\mathbb{R}^P$: **season effect** — league-wide shift in season $j$
- $\varepsilon_n$: **residual** — observation noise

## Covariance and likelihood

Player effects share a low-rank plus diagonal covariance:
$$
\Sigma_a = \Lambda\Lambda^\top + \Psi_a, \qquad \Lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{P\times K},\;K=3
$$
Season and residual covariances are diagonal. Residuals follow Student-$t$ with fitted
degrees of freedom and, in the current production model, playing-time-scaled scale:
$$
\varepsilon_{np} \;\sim\; t\!\left(\nu,\;0,\;\sigma_{e,p}\cdot\sqrt{\tfrac{\bar{m}}{m_n}}\right),
\quad \nu\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(2,0.1)
$$
where $m_n$ is player-season $n$'s minutes and $\bar{m}=1{,}585$ min is the sample median.

## Identification and priors

$\Lambda$ is constrained lower-triangular with positive diagonal (LT-PD), removing
rotational non-identifiability. Factor directions are interpreted post-hoc via PCA of
$\hat\Lambda\hat\Lambda^\top$ (§\ref{sec-interp}). Player effects are parametrised
non-centredly ($a_i = \Lambda\eta_i + \psi_a\odot z_{u,i}$, raw scores centred across
players). Priors: $\Lambda_{kk}\sim\mathrm{HN}(1)$; $\Lambda_{pk}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ for
$p>k$; $\psi_{a,p},\,\sigma_{b,p},\,\sigma_{e,p}\sim\mathrm{HN}(1)$.
NUTS via CmdStan 2.35: 4 chains, 1,000 warmup + 1,000 post-warmup draws, $\delta=0.95$,
PCA-based initialisation.

# Playing-time Heteroskedasticity {#sec-minutes}

## What we found

Performance features are per-90 rates. A player who plays 500 minutes in a season
contributes estimates based on $\approx 6$ matches; one who plays 3,000 minutes contributes
35 matches. The ratio-estimator variance of a per-90 rate scales as $1/m_n$, so low-minute
observations are inherently noisier — yet the prior model used a constant $\sigma_{e,p}$
for all player-seasons.

A quantile diagnostic on the K=3 t-model (constant $\sigma_e$) confirmed this:
**48.9% of the top-200 worst standardised residuals came from the bottom 20th percentile of
playing minutes** (expected: 20%; binomial $p < 10^{-17}$).

```{r}
#| label: fig-minutes-diag
#| fig-cap: "Worst-residual cells vs playing minutes (K=3 t-model, constant $\\sigma_e$). Points in red are in the top-200 worst cells by $|z_{np}|$; points in grey are all other observations. The concentration of extremes at low minutes (left of dashed 20th-percentile line) confirms the heteroskedasticity problem."
#| out-width: "80%"
if (file.exists(fig("30_minutes_vs_residual.png")))
  knitr::include_graphics(fig("30_minutes_vs_residual.png"))
```

## The fix: minutes-scaled residual variance

For Poisson-rate data, $\operatorname{Var}(X/m) = \lambda/m$, so residual SD $\propto m^{-0.5}$
($\phi=0.5$). We modify the likelihood to:
$$
\varepsilon_{np} \;\sim\; t\!\left(\nu,\;0,\;\sigma_{e,p}\cdot\sqrt{\tfrac{\bar{m}}{m_n}}\right)
$$
The reference scale $\sigma_{e,p}$ is at median playing time, so ICC decomposition is
unchanged at $m=\bar{m}$. A second variant estimates $\phi$ directly with prior
$\phi\sim\mathcal{N}(0.5, 0.2)$, testing whether the Poisson prediction $\phi=0.5$ holds.

## Results

| | Constant $\sigma_e$ (prev. model) | Fixed $\phi=0.5$ | Estimated $\phi$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\hat\nu$ | 4.902 | **5.667** | **5.979** |
| 95\% CI for $\nu$ | [4.79, 5.01] | [5.54, 5.80] | [5.83, 6.13] |
| $\hat\phi$ | — | 0.5 (fixed) | **0.366** |
| 95\% CI for $\phi$ | — | — | [0.360, 0.373] |
| $\text{ESS}_\text{bulk}$ ($\nu$) | 2,734 | 2,949 | 2,415 |
| $\hat{R}$ ($\nu$) | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.001 |

The rise in $\hat\nu$ (from 4.90 to 5.67–5.98) confirms the diagnosis: once low-minute
variance is explicitly modelled, the Student-$t$ tail absorbs less unexplained noise.
Student-$t$ remains warranted — $\hat\nu\neq\infty$.

**$\hat\phi = 0.366 < 0.5$**: the estimated exponent is below the Poisson prediction. This
is consistent with *super-Poisson* variance — player heterogeneity is partially absorbed
by the player factor $a_i$, which reduces the residual variance exponent. Fixed $\phi=0.5$
(the Poisson-theory default) is the production model; the estimated variant confirms the
direction and that scaling is real.

## Validation

We re-run the same diagnostic on the minutes-scaled model's residuals:
$$
z^{35}_{np} = \frac{y_{np} - \hat a_{i[n],p} - \hat b_{j[n],p}}
  {\hat\sigma_{e,p}\;\sqrt{\bar{m}/m_n}\;\sqrt{\hat\nu/(\hat\nu-2)}}
$$

| Diagnostic | Before (constant $\sigma_e$) | After (minutes-scaled, $\phi=0.5$) |
|---|---|---|
| Low-minute share in top-200 worst | 48.9\% (88/180 obs) | **8.3\% (14/168 obs)** |
| Binomial $p$ (H1: share $> 20\%$) | $<10^{-17}$ | $>0.999$ |
| Regression slope: max\,$|z|$ $\sim$ log\,min | negative, $p\ll 0.001$ | 0.007, $p=0.97$ |
| Verdict | Over-represented | **CORRECTED** |

```{r}
#| label: fig-minutes-after
#| fig-cap: "Worst-residual cells vs playing minutes after minutes-scaling ($\\phi=0.5$). Red points are top-200 worst cells under the minutes-scaled model. The low-minute concentration is eliminated — the red points are spread uniformly across the minutes range."
#| out-width: "80%"
if (file.exists(fig("35_minutes_vs_residual_34a.png")))
  knitr::include_graphics(fig("35_minutes_vs_residual_34a.png"))
```

# Factor Analysis Results {#sec-rank}

## Rank selection: K=3 chosen from per-K comparison

Following supervisor guidance (*"the CV-based metrics don't decide much; better base the
decision on residuals and the percentage of variability of the PCs of
$\Lambda\Lambda^\top$"*), we compare the K=2, K=3 (and K=4, when the fit completes) full
NUTS Student-$t$ fits on three data-driven criteria the supervisor prescribed:

**(A)** variance share of the principal components of $\hat\Lambda\hat\Lambda^\top$ per K,
**(B)** reliable-loader counts per PC (fixed-reference PCA of §\ref{sec-interp}), and
**(C)** residual adequacy under each fit's own Student-$t$ noise model.

The three fits used for the comparison:

- **K=2** — stage 18 full NUTS Student-$t$ fit ($P=48$, $N=4{,}586$, 4 chains, $\hat\nu=4.882$).
- **K=3** — stage 28 full NUTS Student-$t$ fit ($P=48$, $N=4{,}586$, 4 chains, $\hat\nu=4.902$).
- **K=4** — stage 21 full NUTS Student-$t$ fit, completed 2026-08-26; its Legs A/B/C
  numbers (below) were computed 2026-09-07 after a watcher process that was meant to
  auto-trigger them had died without running (see the Session 15 note in `CLAUDE.md`).

The per-K analyses are driven by two K-parameterised helper scripts
(`scripts/29b_kcompare_residuals.R` for Leg C, `scripts/31b_kcompare_pca.R` for Legs A/B).
Their aggregated outputs live in
`outputs/tables/29b_kcompare_summary.csv` and
`outputs/tables/31b_kcompare_{variance_shares,reliable_counts}.csv`.

### Leg A — Variance share of the PCs of $\hat\Lambda\hat\Lambda^\top$ per K

```{r rank-legA-varshare}
vs <- read.csv("outputs/tables/31b_kcompare_variance_shares.csv")
vs_show <- data.frame(
  K            = vs$K,
  PC           = vs$pc,
  eigenval_LLt = round(vs$eigenval_LLt, 3),
  share_LLt    = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * vs$share_LLt),
  share_Sa     = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * vs$share_Sa)
)
colnames(vs_show) <- c("$K$", "PC",
                       "eigval $\\hat\\Lambda\\hat\\Lambda^\\top$",
                       "share $\\hat\\Lambda\\hat\\Lambda^\\top$",
                       "share $\\hat\\Sigma_a$")
kable(vs_show, booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Per-K variance shares. The **last-PC** row of each K block is the informative one: at K=2 the second (last) PC captures 30.8\\% of $\\hat\\Lambda\\hat\\Lambda^\\top$ variance; at K=3 the third (last) PC captures 10.5\\% — still substantive but sharply diminished. At K=4, PC4 falling to the noise floor is the expected outcome (row appears when stage 21 completes).")
```

**Reading the table for the K decision.** The variance share of each K's *last* PC is
the key comparison — it says how much common structure that extra factor picks up over
the previous K. Concretely:

- K=1 → K=2 adds a second axis capturing 30.8% of common variance (the last PC at K=2). Large — clearly warranted.
- K=2 → K=3 adds a third axis capturing 10.5% of common variance. Smaller but still substantive.
- K=3 → K=4 (pending): if PC4 at K=4 captures a share on the order of a few percent — the noise floor implied by the trailing eigenvalue tail of $\hat\Sigma_a$ (≈ 2%) — that argues for stopping at K=3. The exact number will drive the final call.

The total common variance captured (sum of leading K eigenvalues of
$\hat\Lambda\hat\Lambda^\top$) also grows monotonically with K but should show
diminishing gains:

```{r rank-legA-totals}
tot <- aggregate(eigenval_LLt ~ K, data = vs, sum)
tot$total_eig <- round(tot$eigenval_LLt, 3)
tot$delta <- c(NA, round(diff(tot$eigenval_LLt), 3))
tot_show <- data.frame(
  K = tot$K,
  `Total captured (sum of eigenvalues)` = tot$total_eig,
  `Increment over K-1` = tot$delta,
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(tot_show, booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Total common variance captured per K (sum of the leading K eigenvalues of $\\hat\\Lambda\\hat\\Lambda^\\top$). The `Increment over K-1` column measures the marginal common-variance uptake by the added factor. K=4 increment expected to be substantially smaller than the K=3 increment (2.4).")
```

### Leg B — Reliable-loader count per PC and K

Under the fixed-reference PCA of §\ref{sec-interp} (each draw's loading rotated onto the
eigenbasis of the posterior-mean $\bar{\Lambda}\bar{\Lambda}^\top$, then 90\% marginal
CIs formed), a feature is **reliable** on a given PC if its CI excludes zero.

```{r rank-legB-reliable}
rc <- read.csv("outputs/tables/31b_kcompare_reliable_counts.csv")
rc_show <- data.frame(
  K = rc$K,
  PC = rc$pc,
  `Features` = rc$n_features,
  `Reliable (CI $\\neq 0$)` = rc$n_reliable,
  `Share` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * rc$share_reliable),
  `Max $|$loading$|$` = round(rc$max_abs_load, 3),
  check.names = FALSE
)
colnames(rc_show) <- c("$K$", "PC", "Features", "Reliable ($\\neq 0$)", "Share", "Max $|$loading$|$")
kable(rc_show, booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Reliable-loader count per PC and K. At K=2 the last PC (PC2) has 45/48 reliable loaders (94\\%); at K=3 the last PC (PC3) has 43/48 (90\\%) — a substantively identified third axis. If PC4 at K=4 comes in materially lower (say $<$ 25/48), that is direct evidence the fourth factor is noise-dominated; the row appears when stage 21 completes.")
```

The top-5 reliable loaders per PC at K=3 (the interpretation of the axes) live in
§\ref{sec-interp} (the CI-loading table).

### Leg C — Residual adequacy per K

For each fit we compute standardised residuals $z_{np}$ under that fit's own noise model
($\hat\nu$ estimated per K) and check what share of the $N\times P$ cells exceed the
model's own tail threshold $\tau_{99} = q_{0.995}(t_{\hat\nu}) / \sqrt{\hat\nu/(\hat\nu-2)}$
(expected 1\% under a correctly-specified $t(\hat\nu)$ model), plus a feature-level
skew-triangulation verdict count (rule identical to stage 29).

```{r rank-legC-residuals}
resid_kcmp <- read.csv("outputs/tables/29b_kcompare_summary.csv")
rs_show <- data.frame(
  K                    = resid_kcmp$K,
  `$\\hat\\nu$`        = round(resid_kcmp$nu_hat, 3),
  `$\\tau_{99}$`       = round(resid_kcmp$tau_99, 3),
  `mean $\\Pr(|z|>\\tau_{99})$` = sprintf("%.2f\\%%", 100 * resid_kcmp$mean_frac_gt_tau99),
  `median`             = sprintf("%.2f\\%%", 100 * resid_kcmp$median_frac_gt_tau99),
  `expected under $t$` = sprintf("%.2f\\%%", 100 * resid_kcmp$expected_frac_under_t),
  `\\texttt{unremarkable}`         = resid_kcmp$n_unremarkable,
  `\\texttt{contamination-driven}` = resid_kcmp$n_contamination_driven,
  `\\texttt{skew}`     = resid_kcmp$n_skew_residual,
  `worst $|z|$`        = round(resid_kcmp$worst_cell_zstd, 2),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(rs_show, booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Per-K residual adequacy. Mean feature-level exceedance rates sit below the 1\\% expected under $t(\\hat\\nu)$ at K=2 and K=3 (both models absorb tails adequately). The improvement from K=2 to K=3 in mean $\\Pr(|z|>\\tau_{99})$ is $\\approx 0.03$ pp — small — indicating that residual behaviour alone does not sharply distinguish K=2 from K=3; the residual criterion is a *floor* check, not a discriminator among adequate K. K=4 row appears when stage 21 completes.")
```

**Reading Leg C.** The residual criterion works as a *floor* check: a K is *adequate*
if its mean $\Pr(|z|>\tau_{99})$ sits at or below 1\% (the theoretical expectation
under a well-specified $t(\hat\nu)$ tail). K=2 (0.74\%), K=3 (0.77\%), and K=4 (0.79\%)
all pass, essentially flat. Leg C therefore rules out under-fitting at any K examined
but does not by itself argue for K=3 over K=2 or K=4 — and, as it turns out below, even
Legs A and B do not cleanly settle K=3 vs K=4.

### The K=3 verdict (combining A + B + C) — K=4 does not produce a clean reversal

- **Leg A** — the last PC's common-variance share declines from 30.8\% (K=2) to 10.5\%
  (K=3) to **7.1\% (K=4)**: still declining, but not the drop toward a noise floor
  (~2\%) that motivated running this comparison. The K=2 → K=3 step still adds clearly
  substantive common-variance structure, so K=3 remains preferred over K=2 on this
  criterion; K=3 vs K=4 is a milder, parsimony-flavoured preference rather than a sharp one.
- **Leg B** — 45/48 → 43/48 → **45/48** reliable loaders on the last PC across
  K=2 → K=3 → K=4: **non-monotonic**. PC4 at K=4 is, if anything, as reliably identified
  as PC3 was at K=3, so this criterion gives no reason to prefer K=3 over K=4.
- **Leg C** — K=2, K=3, and K=4 all pass the residual-adequacy floor with closely
  comparable mean exceedance rates (0.74\%, 0.77\%, 0.79\%); this criterion does not
  discriminate at any point in this range.

Taken together: K=3 dominates K=2 on structural criteria (A, B) while matching it on
residual adequacy (C) — that step is clean. The K=3-vs-K=4 step is **not** clean: Leg A
mildly favours K=3, Leg B does not favour either, and Leg C is silent. Combined with the
CV screens below (where K=4 is likewise never clearly dominated), the honest summary is
that the data do not sharply separate K=3 from K=4. K=3 is retained as the production
rank on parsimony grounds — the more economical of two ranks the evidence does not
clearly distinguish — consistent with the supervisor's guidance to close the model at a
qualitatively defensible rank rather than chase an open-ended search through
successively higher, likely similarly ambiguous, comparisons.

### Cross-validation is inconclusive — honest disclosure

The two CV screens do **not** unambiguously select K=3:

- **Pathfinder screening (`outputs/rank_selection/real_data_elpd.csv`, $K=0,\ldots,8$)**.
  In the truncated $K\leq 4$ view (Fig. below), ELPD rises to K=3 and reverses at K=4 —
  consistent with K=3. However, the *full-range* Pathfinder is non-monotonic and the
  argmax is at K=5 (elpd $=-3.107$ vs K=3's $-3.239$, a local dip). This is
  Pathfinder's variational-approximation instability at higher K, not a substantive
  K=5 signal, but it means the Pathfinder ELPD alone cannot select the rank.

- **Player-holdout CV ($K=1,\ldots,6$, `outputs/tables/32_player_holdout_elpd.csv`)**.
  Argmax at **K=6** on both metrics (elpd$_{\text{base}}$ $=-34{,}729.5$ at K=6 vs
  $-34{,}737.2$ at K=3; elpd$_{\text{mv}}$ $=-34{,}184.4$ at K=6 vs $-34{,}211.0$ at
  K=3). K=4 also beats K=3 on the minutes-scaled metric ($-34{,}209.8$). Reported
  per-K SEs are Pathfinder-draw variances, which under-represent posterior uncertainty;
  the ranking should be read as *flat across $K\in\{2,\ldots,6\}$* rather than as
  favouring a single K.

- **PSIS-LOO K=3 vs K=2** — $\Delta$ELPD $= 1{,}244$ with SE $= 1{,}271$ (i.e., the
  difference is smaller than its own SE) and 99.4\% of points have Pareto-$k>0.5$
  (`outputs/tables/C_loo_k2_vs_k3.csv`). Directional only.

```{r}
#| label: fig-elpd-rank
#| fig-cap: "Pathfinder ELPD per held-out value, truncated $K=0,\\ldots,4$ view (rebuilt data, $N=4{,}586$, $P=48$). The circled K=3 is the adopted rank on qualitative grounds; the ordering shown is consistent with that choice, but the full-range Pathfinder ($K=0,\\ldots,8$) is non-monotonic and is *not* load-bearing for the K=3 decision."
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 3.2
elpd_full <- read.csv(rs("real_data_elpd.csv"))
elpd <- elpd_full[elpd_full$rank <= 4, ]
ggplot(elpd, aes(x = rank, y = elpd_per_value)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2166ac", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#2166ac") +
  geom_point(data = elpd[elpd$rank == 3, ], size = 5, colour = "#d73027",
             shape = 1, stroke = 2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.3f", elpd_per_value)), vjust = -1.0, size = 3.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:4) +
  expand_limits(y = max(elpd$elpd_per_value) + 0.04) +
  labs(x = "Factor rank K", y = "ELPD per held-out value",
       caption = "Circle = adopted K=3. Truncated view for illustration; full K=0..8 is non-monotonic.") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

K=7--8 not computed (wall-clock constraint).")

### Final rank verdict

**K=3** is the production rank. The comparative evidence in Legs A/B/C above shows:
K=3 dominates K=2 on structural criteria (last-PC common-variance share drops from 30.8\%
to 10.5\% but PC3 is still 90\% reliable-loaded); K=2 and K=3 match on residual adequacy
(both below the 1\% floor). That step is clean. The K=3-vs-K=4 step, now that stage 21
has completed and been analysed, is **not** clean: PC4's variance share (7.1\%) is small
but not at a noise floor, and its reliable-loader count (45/48) is not lower than PC3's
at K=3 (43/48) — the null prediction that motivated stopping at K=3 did not fully
materialise. K=3 is retained regardless, on parsimony grounds given a genuinely
ambiguous K=3-vs-K=4 comparison, matching the supervisor's guidance to close the model
rather than continue chasing successively higher ranks. The CV screens above are
consistent with this call but are themselves inconclusive across $K \in \{2,\ldots,6\}$
(K=4 included), so they do not carry the argument either way.

## Factor loadings with posterior credible intervals {#sec-interp}

The lower-triangular loadings $\Lambda$ are an identification device and are not
interpretable directly. We apply PCA to the posterior-mean common variance matrix
$\hat\Lambda\hat\Lambda^\top$ to obtain rotation-invariant factor directions.
Variance shares:

| | PC1 | PC2 | PC3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\hat\Lambda\hat\Lambda^\top$ (common) | 61.8\% | 27.7\% | 10.5\% |
| $\hat\Sigma_a = \hat\Lambda\hat\Lambda^\top + \hat\Psi_a$ (total player) | 45.6\% | 20.7\% | 8.1\% |

The gap between the two rows is the per-feature uniqueness $\hat\Psi_a$: approximately
25\% of total player variance is feature-specific and not captured by the shared factors.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sigma-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Variance shares per PC for $\\hat\\Lambda\\hat\\Lambda^\\top$ vs $\\hat\\Sigma_a = \\hat\\Lambda\\hat\\Lambda^\\top + \\hat\\Psi_a$. The gap is the uniqueness $\\hat\\Psi_a$."
#| out-width: "68%"
if (file.exists(fig("31_sigma_a_vs_llambda_comparison.png")))
  knitr::include_graphics(fig("31_sigma_a_vs_llambda_comparison.png"))
```

**New in this version:** posterior CIs on the loadings are now available from draws-level
PCA. The figure below propagates the $\Lambda$ posterior to give 90\% marginal CIs on each
rotated loading. A feature is **reliable** (solid) if its CI excludes zero.

**Fixed-reference PCA (methods).** The eigenvectors of a per-draw $\Lambda_s\Lambda_s^\top$
can rotate freely across posterior draws — the leading two- or three-dimensional
subspace is identified by the data, but its internal orientation is not. Per supervisor
guidance, we therefore fix the reference orientation to the eigendecomposition of the
posterior mean $\bar{\Lambda}\bar{\Lambda}^\top$ (SVD $\to V_{\text{ref}}$, sign-anchored
via the largest-magnitude entry per column), and each draw's loading vector is projected
onto this fixed $V_{\text{ref}}$ before the 90\% marginal CI is formed
(`scripts/31_pca_with_ci.R`). This is a first-order (mean-rotation) approximation of a
fully Procrustes-aligned per-draw CI; the *reliable/unreliable* flag we report is robust
to the approximation because it depends on the CI's *sign*, not its width.

```{r}
#| out-width: "100%"
if (file.exists(fig("31_pca_loading_ci_plot.png")))
  knitr::include_graphics(fig("31_pca_loading_ci_plot.png"))
```

```{r ci-loader-table}
top_rel <- do.call(rbind, lapply(paste0("PC", 1:3), function(pc) {
  sub <- rel[rel$pc == pc, ]
  sub <- sub[order(-abs(sub$loading)), ][seq_len(min(5, nrow(sub))), ]
  data.frame(
    PC      = pc,
    Feature = gsub("_", " ", gsub("^per90_|^rate_", "", sub$feature)),
    Group   = sub$group,
    Loading = round(sub$loading, 3),
    `CI lo` = round(sub$ci_lo, 3),
    `CI hi` = round(sub$ci_hi, 3),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}))
kable(top_rel, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Top 5 reliable loaders per PC (CI excludes zero). Positive PC1 = defensive; negative PC1 = attacking. PC2: positive = technical/pass; negative = aerial/physical. PC3: positive = possession quality; negative = wide/direct.")
```

## Player profiles and comparisons {#sec-profiles}

### Construction

**Step 1 — Player effects.** The starting point is $\hat{a}_{i,p}$, the posterior mean
player effect for player $i$ and feature $p$. These are extracted directly from the fitted
model: because the model decomposes each observation as
$y_n = a_{i[n]} + b_{j[n]} + \varepsilon_n$, the player effect has already had season-wide
shifts ($b_j$) and residual noise ($\varepsilon_n$) removed. What remains is each player's
stable latent identity in the original 48-dimensional Z-scored feature space — not a
dimension-reduced projection.

**Step 2 — Loading-weighted group composite.** The 48 features are assigned to eight
groups (Table below). For each group $g$ and player $i$:
$$
\text{composite}_{i,g}
  = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{p\,\in\, g} |\lambda_{p,1}|\,\hat{a}_{i,p}}
         {\displaystyle\sum_{p\,\in\, g} |\lambda_{p,1}|}
$$
where $\lambda_{p,1}$ is the PC1 loading of feature $p$ from the PCA of
$\hat\Lambda\hat\Lambda^\top$ (§\ref{sec-interp}). Using absolute loading magnitude
as weight gives more influence to features that explain more inter-player covariance in
the factor model — connecting the radar directly to the model's structure. Features absent
from the loading table fall back to weight 1.

One practical adjustment was required: the two original "Shooting rates" features
(\texttt{rate\_shots\_on\_target}, \texttt{rate\_goal\_conversion}) were dropped from the
model in the feature-selection step (low ICC). The SHOOT spoke is therefore populated by
reassigning the finishing features from the Attacking output group —
\texttt{per90\_goals}, \texttt{per90\_shots}, \texttt{per90\_xg\_shot},
\texttt{per90\_head\_shots} — while the ATTACK spoke retains the creation and box-presence
features (\texttt{per90\_touch\_in\_box}, \texttt{per90\_assists},
\texttt{per90\_xg\_assist}). This gives a more informative split: ATTACK measures how
much a player creates chances; SHOOT measures how much they finish them.

**Step 3 — Percentile conversion.** Each composite is ranked among all 1,529 outfield
players and converted to a 0--100 scale:
$$
\text{pct}_{i,g} = \frac{\mathrm{rank}(\text{composite}_{i,g})}{1{,}529}\times 100
$$
A score of 90 means the player's loading-weighted effect in group $g$ exceeds 90\% of the
La Liga outfield pool. 50 is the median player; the scale is the same for all pairs.

**What this is not.** The spoke values are not PC scores (those appear only in the
scatter plot and similarity metric), not raw statistics, and not ICC values. The radars
show a player's purified, season-adjusted group fingerprint on the model's own scale,
converted to a percentile for legibility.

**Direction correction.** For features where a higher raw value is worse, the sign is
flipped before computing the composite, so that 100th percentile always means "better":
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textit{Discipline}: \texttt{per90\_fouls} and \texttt{per90\_yellow\_cards} are negated
        (fewer = better). \texttt{per90\_fouls\_suffered} is excluded from this spoke entirely —
        being fouled is position-dependent (attackers are fouled far more than defenders) and
        does not reflect disciplinary behaviour.
  \item \textit{Defending}: \texttt{per90\_losses}, \texttt{per90\_own\_half\_losses}, and
        \texttt{per90\_dangerous\_own\_half\_losses} are negated (fewer ball losses = better
        defending).
\end{itemize}
All other features are kept as-is; higher Z-score already corresponds to more of a
desirable quantity (more recoveries, more dribbles, higher pass completion, etc.).


### Player similarity

The radar compares players within a single group at a time. For a global similarity
score, we use a different (and complementary) representation.

Each player's posterior-mean effect $\hat{a}_i\in\mathbb{R}^{48}$ is projected onto
the three PCA eigenvectors of $\hat\Lambda\hat\Lambda^\top$, giving scores
$(s_{i,1}, s_{i,2}, s_{i,3})$ that summarise the player's archetype in a three-number
summary. These are the PC scores shown in the scatter plot. Each PC is then standardised
to unit variance across the 1,529 players before computing distance, so all three
dimensions contribute equally regardless of their raw scale. The similarity between
players $i$ and $i'$ is:
$$
d(i,i') = \left\lVert
  \begin{pmatrix} \tilde s_{i,1}\\ \tilde s_{i,2}\\ \tilde s_{i,3} \end{pmatrix}
  -
  \begin{pmatrix} \tilde s_{i',1}\\ \tilde s_{i',2}\\ \tilde s_{i',3} \end{pmatrix}
\right\rVert_2, \qquad
\tilde s_{i,k} = \frac{s_{i,k} - \bar{s}_k}{\mathrm{sd}(s_k)}
$$
A distance of 1 unit $\approx$ one SD of combined-archetype separation across the pool.

```{r similarity-table}
if (file.exists(tbl("37_player_similarity_top10.csv"))) {
  sim      <- read.csv(tbl("37_player_similarity_top10.csv"))
  show_pls <- c("L. Messi", "Sergio Ramos", "Sergio Busquets", "K. Benzema")
  sim_show <- sim[sim$player_name %in% show_pls & sim$rank <= 5,
                  c("player_name", "rank", "similar_player", "distance")]
  sim_show$distance <- round(sim_show$distance, 3)
  colnames(sim_show) <- c("Player", "Rank", "Similar player", "Distance")
  kable(sim_show, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
        caption = "Top-5 nearest neighbours in archetype space for four named players. Messi's nearest neighbour is Neymar (dist\\,=\\,1.74); Ramos's is Piqué (dist\\,=\\,0.16).")
}
```

# Model Fit Summary {#sec-fit}

## Student-$t$ tail evolution {#sec-tails}

| Quantity | Pre-rebuild | K=3, constant $\sigma_e$ | K=3, minutes-scaled |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\hat\nu$ | 2.95 | **4.90** | **5.67** |
| 95\% CI | [2.91, 2.99] | [4.79, 5.01] | [5.54, 5.80] |
| $\text{Var}(\varepsilon)/\sigma_e^2$ | 1.93 | **1.53** | **1.54** |
| $\tau_{99}$ (in $\sigma_e$ units) | 3.371 | **3.135** | **3.06** |

Pre-rebuild $\hat\nu=2.95$ reflected GK contamination and feature right-skew, not genuine
heavy tails. After GK exclusion and transforms: $\hat\nu=4.90$. After minutes scaling:
$\hat\nu=5.67$ — the tail absorbs less residual heteroskedasticity. Student-$t$ remains
appropriate ($\hat\nu\neq\infty$; genuine extreme seasons still occur).

## Sampler diagnostics

```{r diag-table}
dc <- read.csv(tbl("28_diagnostics_cache.csv"))

nu_row    <- dc[dc$param == "nu", ]
psi_rows  <- dc[grepl("^psi_a\\.", dc$param), ]
sige_rows <- dc[grepl("^sigma_e\\.", dc$param), ]
sigb_rows <- dc[grepl("^sigma_b\\.", dc$param), ]
llt_row   <- dc[dc$param == "LLt.1.10", ]
llt_all   <- dc[grepl("^Lambda_a\\.|^LLt\\.", dc$param), ]

diag_smry <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c(
    "$\\hat{\\nu}$ (degrees of freedom)",
    "$\\psi_{a,p}$ (48 uniqueness)",
    "$\\sigma_{e,p}$ (48 residual SD)",
    "$\\sigma_{b,p}$ (48 season SD)",
    "$\\Lambda_a$ loadings (144 entries)",
    "$\\text{LLt}_{[1,10]}$ (mixing bellwether)"
  ),
  `ESS (median)` = c(
    round(nu_row$ess_bulk),
    round(median(psi_rows$ess_bulk, na.rm=TRUE)),
    round(median(sige_rows$ess_bulk, na.rm=TRUE)),
    round(median(sigb_rows$ess_bulk, na.rm=TRUE)),
    round(median(llt_all$ess_bulk, na.rm=TRUE)),
    round(llt_row$ess_bulk)
  ),
  `ESS (min)` = c(
    round(nu_row$ess_bulk),
    round(min(psi_rows$ess_bulk, na.rm=TRUE)),
    round(min(sige_rows$ess_bulk, na.rm=TRUE)),
    round(min(sigb_rows$ess_bulk, na.rm=TRUE)),
    round(min(llt_all$ess_bulk, na.rm=TRUE)),
    round(llt_row$ess_bulk)
  ),
  `Rhat (max)` = c(
    round(nu_row$rhat, 3),
    round(max(psi_rows$rhat, na.rm=TRUE), 3),
    round(max(sige_rows$rhat, na.rm=TRUE), 3),
    round(max(sigb_rows$rhat, na.rm=TRUE), 3),
    round(max(llt_all$rhat, na.rm=TRUE), 3),
    round(llt_row$rhat, 3)
  ),
  Verdict = c("PASS", "PASS", "PASS", "PASS",
              ifelse(max(llt_all$rhat, na.rm=TRUE) < 1.05, "PASS", "BORDERLINE"),
              ifelse(llt_row$ess_bulk > 200 & llt_row$rhat < 1.01, "PASS", "BORDERLINE")),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(diag_smry, booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "K=3 t-model diagnostic summary (4 chains × 1,000 draws). Threshold: ESS > 200, Rhat < 1.01. The $\\text{LLt}_{[1,10]}$ entry (goals $\\times$ passes, Factor 1) was the historical mixing bottleneck: ESS rose from 24 (pre-rebuild) to 237 (K=3 post-rebuild) via GK exclusion, feature transforms, and K=3 giving passes its own dedicated loading.")
```

## Explained variability (ICC)

For each feature, ICC decomposes total variance into player, season, and residual components:
$$
\text{ICC}_\text{player} = \frac{\Sigma_{a,pp}}{\Sigma_{a,pp} + \Sigma_{b,pp} + \Sigma_{e,pp}},
\quad \Sigma_{a,pp} = \Lambda_{p\cdot}\Lambda_{p\cdot}^\top + \psi_{a,p}^2
$$

```{r}
#| label: fig-icc-barchart
#| fig-cap: "ICC decomposition for all 48 features (K=2 Normal model, rebuilt data), ranked by player ICC. Blue = stable player skill, orange = season signal, grey = residual noise."
#| out-width: "96%"
knitr::include_graphics(fig("16_icc_ranked_barchart.png"))
```

```{r icc-top-table}
icc    <- read.csv(tbl("16_icc_summary.csv"))
groups <- as.data.frame(feature_group_lookup())
icc_top <- merge(
  icc[order(-icc$icc_player), c("feature","icc_player","icc_season","icc_residual")][1:10, ],
  groups, by = "feature", all.x = TRUE
)
icc_top$group   <- ifelse(is.na(icc_top$group), "Other", icc_top$group)
icc_top         <- icc_top[order(-icc_top$icc_player), ]
icc_top$feature <- gsub("_", " ", gsub("^per90_|^rate_", "", icc_top$feature))
icc_top[, c("icc_player","icc_season","icc_residual")] <-
  round(icc_top[, c("icc_player","icc_season","icc_residual")] * 100, 1)
kable(icc_top[, c("feature","group","icc_player","icc_season","icc_residual")],
      booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Feature", "Group", "Player ICC (%)", "Season ICC (%)", "Residual ICC (%)"),
      caption = "Top 10 features by player ICC (K=2 Normal model, rebuilt P=48). ICC from the K=3 t-model is structurally identical at $m=\\bar{m}$; numerical recomputation is pending.")
```

## Model comparisons

```{r comparison-table}
comp <- data.frame(
  Comparison = c(
    "Low-rank $K=2$ vs diagonal $K=0$",
    "$t$-errors vs Gaussian ($K=2$, pre-rebuild)",
    "Low-rank $K=3$ vs $K=2$ (Pathfinder)",
    "Low-rank $K=3$ vs $K=2$ (PSIS-LOO)",
    "Low-rank $K=3$ vs diagonal $K=0$ (LOO, rebuilt)",
    "Minutes-scaled ($\\hat\\phi=0.5$) vs constant $\\sigma_e$"
  ),
  `$\\Delta$ELPD` = c("$+3{,}724$", "$+11{,}668$", "$+12{,}125$*", "$+1{,}244$**", "$+5{,}820.2$", "n/a††"),
  `SE` = c("187", "554", "—", "1,271", "343.5", "—"),
  Source = c(
    "PSIS-LOO ($P=53$, $N=4944$)",
    "PSIS-LOO ($P=53$, $N=4944$)",
    "Pathfinder screening ($P=48$, $N=4586$)",
    "PSIS-LOO ($P=48$, $N=4586$)",
    "PSIS-LOO ($P=48$, $N=4586$); directional (Pareto-$k>0.7$ for ~90\\% of points)",
    "$\\hat\\nu$ rises 4.90$\\to$5.67; low-min share 48.9\\%$\\to$8.3\\%"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(comp, booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Comparison", "$\\Delta$ELPD", "SE", "Source/Note"),
      caption = "All model comparisons. * Pathfinder: variational approximation; direction reliable but a single-K numeric optimum is not (see §\\ref{sec-rank}). ** PSIS-LOO: $\\Delta$ELPD $<$ SE and 99.4\\% Pareto-$k>0.5$; directional only. †† LOO not computed for minutes-scaled model (compute\\_log\\_lik=0); qualitative evidence from $\\hat\\nu$ rise and diagnostic.")
```

The low-rank structure is strongly supported over diagonal both on the pre-rebuild data
(20 SE) and, now, on the rebuilt $P=48$/$N=4{,}586$ data directly (17 SE; row 5 above),
and Student-$t$ residuals are strongly warranted. For rank selection, K=3 is adopted on
qualitative grounds (§\ref{sec-rank}, Legs A/B/C) rather than by $\Delta$ELPD: the
Pathfinder, player-holdout CV, and PSIS-LOO comparisons among $K \geq 1$ are *consistent*
with K=3 but do not by themselves single out a K within the neighbourhood — see the
honest disclosure in §\ref{sec-rank}, including the K=3-vs-K=4 comparison, which is not
as clean as originally hoped. The minutes-scaled extension is validated by the diagnostic
(§\ref{sec-minutes}) even without a formal LOO comparison.

# Open Questions {#sec-open}

1. **Low-rank vs diagonal comparison on rebuilt data — resolved (2026-09-07).** The
   diagonal baseline (stage 03) had already been refit on the current data
   ($P=48$, $N=4{,}586$); the LOO comparison against the K=3 production model itself had
   just never been run. Now computed: $\Delta$ELPD $=+5{,}820.2$ (SE $343.5$),
   confirming the low-rank structure is strongly supported on the current data too (not
   just the pre-rebuild dataset). One wrinkle worth recording: the first extraction
   attempt used stage 28's own posterior-summary CSVs and returned a degenerate,
   all-zero result — its `log_lik` columns are declared in the header but were never
   populated (`compute_log_lik=0` at fit time). The fix was to reuse the real log_lik
   already computed via `generate_quantities()` for the K=2-vs-K=3 comparison
   (`fits/csv/block_c_gq/k3/`), which needed no new Stan run.

2. **Factor archetype labels based on posterior CIs.** The group radar and cluster labels
   (§\ref{sec-interp}) are based on the posterior-mean PCA rotation. The CI-filtered
   loading plot now shows which loadings are reliably non-zero, but the archetype labels
   for the player scatter have not yet been updated to reflect this — a minor
   presentation refinement, not affecting the substantive interpretation.

3. **Team-season effects.** A team-season effect $c_{t[n]}\in\mathbb{R}^P$ would separate
   manager/tactical system effects from stable player identity. Player-team mapping is
   available in the raw data; this is the main modelling extension to consider once the
   current model is closed.

---

# Appendix: Outlier Study {#sec-outliers}

Standardised residuals computed for all $N\times P=220{,}128$ cells of the K=3 t-model
(constant $\sigma_e$, posterior-mean effects):
$$
z_{np} = \frac{y_{np} - \hat{a}_{i[n],p} - \hat{b}_{j[n],p}}{\hat\sigma_{e,p}\sqrt{\hat\nu/(\hat\nu-2)}},
\quad \tau_{99} = \frac{q_{0.995}(t_{\hat\nu})}{\sqrt{\hat\nu/(\hat\nu-2)}} \approx 3.135
$$

```{r}
#| label: fig-p99-bar
#| fig-cap: "p99 of $|z_{np}|$ for each of the 48 features. Dashed line = $\\tau_{99}=3.135$ (model's own 99th-pct threshold at $\\hat{\\nu}=4.902$). Features above the line have heavier tails than the fitted model predicts."
#| out-width: "96%"
if (file.exists(fig("29_residual_p99_barchart.png")))
  knitr::include_graphics(fig("29_residual_p99_barchart.png"))
```

```{r feat-smry-table}
if (file.exists(tbl("29_residual_feature_summary.csv")) &&
    file.exists(tbl("29_residual_skew_triangulation.csv"))) {
  fs  <- read.csv(tbl("29_residual_feature_summary.csv"))
  tri <- read.csv(tbl("29_residual_skew_triangulation.csv"))
  fs  <- merge(fs, tri[, c("feature", "verdict")], by = "feature", all.x = TRUE)
  fs_show <- head(fs[order(-fs$p99_abs), ], 12)
  fs_show$feature       <- gsub("_", " ", gsub("^per90_|^rate_", "", fs_show$feature))
  fs_show$p50_abs       <- round(fs_show$p50_abs, 3)
  fs_show$p99_abs       <- round(fs_show$p99_abs, 3)
  fs_show$frac_gt_tau99 <- paste0(round(100 * fs_show$frac_gt_tau99, 2), "%")
  fs_show$verdict       <- ifelse(is.na(fs_show$verdict), "—", fs_show$verdict)
  kable(fs_show[, c("feature", "group", "p50_abs", "p99_abs", "frac_gt_tau99", "verdict")],
        booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
        col.names = c("Feature", "Group", "p50 |z|", "p99 |z|", "Frac > τ₉₉", "Verdict"),
        caption = "Top 12 features by p99 of standardised residuals (K=3 t-model). Contamination-driven = genuine player-level outliers (high ICC); skew-residual = residual right-skew after transform.")
}
```

```{r worst-cells}
if (file.exists(tbl("29_residual_worst_cells.csv"))) {
  wc <- read.csv(tbl("29_residual_worst_cells.csv"))
  wc_show <- head(wc, 20)
  wc_show$feature <- gsub("_", " ", gsub("^per90_|^rate_", "", wc_show$feature))
  wc_show$z_std <- round(wc_show$z_std, 2)
  wc_show$season_label <- c(
    "12/13","13/14","14/15","15/16","16/17","17/18",
    "18/19","19/20","20/21","21/22","22/23","23/24"
  )[wc_show$season_index]
  kable(wc_show[, c("rank", "player_name", "season_label", "feature", "z_std")],
        booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
        col.names = c("Rank", "Player", "Season", "Feature", "$z$"),
        escape = FALSE,
        caption = "Top 20 outlier cells by $|z_{np}|$ (K=3 t-model, $\\tau_{99}=3.135$). These residuals are large relative to the model's own tail expectations — genuine extreme seasons or persistent modelling gaps.")
}
```
